lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ask a computer for movies like The Matrix and it has to answer three different questions at once. Which one are you really asking?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Three questions? I'd have said one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine's teaching thread splits them: films that feel like a plot description, people who rated like you, and why these titles were picked. Mixing them without saying which kind of vector you used is, in his words, how demos lie.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Part one is PostgreSQL with pgvector. Combine title, year, genres, cast and summary, encode it with Sentence Transformers, and store the vector next to the normal columns. Nearest neighbours become a plain SQL ORDER BY with a LIMIT.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Qdrant with the MovieLens datasets, behind a FastAPI app. One path is dense search over title and genre text. The other is a sparse search on ratings: find the twenty nearest users and add up their ratings for movies you haven't seen.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Was anything surprising when he reread the code?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The movie vectors don't contain plots at all, just titles plus genres or release dates. And the query uses raw one-to-five ratings while the stored ones are centered, so a one-star rating still pulls toward people who liked the movie.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Retrieval-augmented generation with LangChain and a local Ollama model, grounded on the same rows. The saved notebook output fails politely: invalid SQL, warnings about vector columns, and timeouts on heavy models.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So generators drift unless you constrain them.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's his takeaway. Embed, store, find neighbours, three times, with three meanings of neighbour. The full write-up has the diagram and the notebooks.
